text: The charming residential building was erected in 1909 and is situated in a scenic and secluded location at the end of a road in Valinge. The property has a rich and varied history; over the decades, the house has served as a safe home for several generations of local families, but it has also housed newer businesses. Today, the property (with the historical designation Rygg 3:7, now Rygg 24) comprises the residential house along with three barns, and is a vibrant place offering overnight accommodation as well as hosting courses, events, and festive celebrations.

Sometime during the 1960s, the property was taken over by a Danish man (and his wife/partner). In connection with the change of ownership, an extensive total renovation was carried out, and during their time on the farm they operated a dog boarding kennel, among other things. Following this period, the house eventually stood empty due to a probate dispute, which unfortunately led to its deterioration – before the current owners took over, put in a tremendous amount of hard work, and brought Lunden back to life.

Arthur William Sixten Nilsson was born on March 23, 1910, in Abild and moved into the house on November 8, 1943. He worked as a milk recorder/control assistant, and the household also included his wife Junis Linnéa (née Gustavsson), born on June 4, 1914, in Varberg. They married on November 20, 1937, and had daughters Siv Elsa Anita (born February 25, 1938), Gerd Harriet Irène (born December 19, 1940), and Gudrun Elsie Margaretha (born November 29, 1945). The family also included their son Gösta, who was born in the 1950s and is therefore not listed in the older parish records. Arthur passed away on June 13, 1986, and Junis on February 1, 1998; the couple rests together at St. Jörgen's Cemetery. It was likely during Arthur's time, around the 1960s, that the farm was transferred to the Danish man.

Before Arthur and his family took over, the house was owned and occupied by the carpenter Johan Andersson, born on June 1, 1898, in Valinge. He was married to Anna Hildegard (née Johansson), born on July 15, 1902, in Valinge. The couple married on February 10, 1922, and it was in connection with the wedding that they took over the property. They had two daughters: Astrid Junia (born March 4, 1922, died March 12, 1997) and Inga-Marianne (born December 6, 1935). Johan's father Sven also lived with them in the house until his death in 1938. On October 20, 1944, the entire family moved out to settle in Lindberg. Johan passed away in 1968 and Anna on February 28, 1993. Johan is buried in Valinge alongside his wife and their eldest daughter Astrid.

Before Johan took over, the house was owned by his father, Sven Edvard Andersson, born on February 9, 1858, in Valinge and deceased on December 30, 1938. It was Sven who had the house built on November 25, 1909. He lived there with his wife Hilma Maria Johansdotter, born on May 26, 1856, in Lindberg and deceased on July 4, 1926. They had married on November 23, 1881, and had their son Johan. The household was also home to Augusta Josefina Andersdotter (born March 6, 1856, died June 10, 1918), who was likely a sister of Sven. Sven is buried in Valinge together with his wife and two other female relatives, possibly sisters.

Going even further back in time, we find Sven's father, Carl Petter Larsson (born August 6, 1830, in Valinge), who was a crofter at Rygg 4. Sven's mother was Johanna Andersdotter, born on December 28, 1818, in Valinge. In addition to Sven, the children included sister Matilda (born October 23, 1863) and brother Johan Anton (born June 22, 1856), who later moved to Rolfstorp in 1875. When Sven's mother Johanna passed away on April 16, 1883, his father Carl Petter remarried Britta Christina Bengtsdotter (born September 24, 1833) from Lindberg.

history.heading2: Historical Events and Fates in Valinge Parish
text: One of the major milestones in the parish's modern history was when the old medieval stone church in Valinge was demolished in 1886. In 1891–1892, the current church was completed in a proud Neo-Romanesque style. Construction was a major event for the entire community, requiring extensive efforts and transport from all the crofters and farmers of the parish. However, the church tower was preserved from an earlier renovation in 1840 and still bears King Karl XIV Johan's initials (CXJVJ) in wrought iron on its facade.

During the 19th century, the land consolidation reform ('laga skifte') was carried out in Valinge parish, fundamentally altering the entire cultural landscape. Previously, houses were clustered together in village centers, but with the reform, villages were broken up, and families moved their dwellings and outbuildings directly out to their assigned land parcels. It was this historical reform that laid the foundation for individual small properties – like Lunden at Rygg – to emerge and be partitioned off.

Everyday life in the countryside was also marked by hardships and illness. On March 20, 1814, four children died during the Varberg area's epidemics of whooping cough and measles – childhood diseases that claimed many young lives in Halland during this period. In Valinge, Lundby was among the places affected when the ten-month-old infant boy Johannes Börjesson passed away from whooping cough.

The parish's older history also includes dramatic individual court cases. In the local court records archive, an incident from the days of the Great Northern War in 1711 is documented, where a baggage train driver in Valinge suffered a tragic death that was brought before the district court. It is one of the oldest individual crime and tragedy notices documented in the area's local history research.

During World War II, Valinge unexpectedly found itself at the center of events. On October 10, 1943, a large Allied bomber of the type Liberator Mk.III (belonging to the British Royal Air Force) crashed in a field in the parish. The plane was returning home from a special mission when it ran out of fuel. The entire crew of seven Polish aviators managed to save themselves by parachuting north of Rolfstorp before the abandoned aircraft crashed.

In 1959, the community was shaken by the so-called Valinge Strike, when church caretaker Gustaf Nilsson went on strike. This led to a prolonged and bitter trade union conflict that attracted widespread attention. The strike became famous for its dramatic occurrences, where strikebreakers ('scabs') reportedly dug graves under the cover of darkness so that funerals could be carried out despite the blockade.

In recent times, visitors and friends who have stayed overnight or looked after the property have reported strange and unusual occurrences on the farm. Several people have both heard and seen phenomena suggesting a continued presence on the property. Among other things, witnesses have noticed a man who appears to walk around, fixing things and keeping order in the house – closing doors left open and making sounds in the kitchen as if someone were doing the dishes. These experiences have mainly occurred when the owners were away and others were minding the farm, as though the man is also there to look after the property and keep a watchful eye over Lunden.
